| ST10 cycle time stepped up at a shift start and stays at the new level; process signals normal | Timer or dwell parameter changed at the changeover (wrong value, wrong recipe, or a trial value left active) | Compare the active parameter set with the last approved copy; check the parameter log for the shift start | Restore the approved value under change control; record the deviation |

Hydraulic wear develops over hours to days, not at a changeover. Four failure modes are common: internal pump leakage, a sluggish (lagging) switching valve, loss of accumulator precharge, and loss of cooler efficiency. Each moves pressure, motor current, oil temperature, vibration and cycle time in its own pattern; use Table 6-3 to tell them apart. All four lengthen the press cycle, which starves the stations downstream.

Regulated gun air (`air_pressure_bar`) normally sits at 5.6 bar within 5.3 to 5.9 bar. Below 5 bar the cell raises a low-air alarm; at 4.6 bar the supply-air interlock stops the cell. Gun force alarms (A-ST20-GUN-FRC, A-ST30-GUN-FRC) can appear as the air falls.

citations.quote: When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows. The weld cells see their regulated gun air fall shortly after; gun force alarms follow, and when gun air reaches each cell's own low limit (see the weld cell manual) the supply-air interlock stops that cell.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.
A fall in gun air pressure at ST20 and ST30 at the same time, after the header pressure has fallen, places the cause in the air supply, not in the weld cells.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. citations.quote: Tip resistance that rises in a straight line over several hours, together with a stepping weld current, is the signature of electrode tip wear, not of a controller fault.

If tip resistance rises at one weld cell only, the tips or the tip dresser at that cell are the cause; if weld faults start at ST20 right after a press changeover, check the parts first (see Section 6.7).

Tip resistance (`tip_resistance_mohm`) climbs steadily over hours from about 0.15 mOhm towards the 0.185 mOhm alarm limit as the tip faces pick up coating material and oxide (which raises contact resistance) and lose their shape, while the current stepper raises weld current (`weld_current_ka`) to compensate. Rejects at ST60 follow later, once the weld nuggets become undersized. Servo temperature, gun air pressure and cycle time stay normal.

If temperature reaches 72 degC, the cell issues an over-temperature alarm, followed by a total cell trip at 80 degC.

citations.quote: Hydraulic wear develops over hours to days, not at a changeover. citations.quote: A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
Check drop-leg fittings and quick couplings at the weld cells first; they account for most leaks on this header.

Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. The 72 degC alarm comes before the 80 degC trip.

| Trip S-ST20-SRV-OT or S-ST30-SRV-OT at 80 degC | Sustained overheating not corrected at the alarm stage | Check coolant flow (ST30), the cabinet fan and the gun mechanics for binding | Let the drive cool; restart only after the cause is found |

citations.quote: The normal range is the band the equipment stays in during normal production. An alarm limit raises a warning and the station keeps running; a trip limit stops the station. A dash means the limit is not used.
| S-ST10-HYD-FLT | ST10 Press: hydraulic fault, press stopped | Hydraulic protection; see Section 6.3 |

A normal production stop is executed from the control interface at the conclusion of a run or shift. Halting the station de-energizes the electric pump motor, centers the directional valves, and parks the press slide in its resting position.

Operating personnel must understand that a normal production stop does not establish an energy-isolated state. High electrical voltage remains present inside control enclosures, and pressurized hydraulic fluid stays stored within the bladder accumulator and main fluid circuits.

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

Tip resistance that rises in a straight line over several hours, together with a stepping weld current, is the signature of electrode tip wear, not of a controller fault.

Typical signature. Tip resistance (tip_resistance_mohm) climbs steadily over hours from about 0.15 mOhm towards the 0.185 mOhm alarm limit as the tip faces pick up coating material and oxide (which raises contact resistance) and lose their shape, while the current stepper raises weld current (weld_current_ka) to compensate.

citations.quote: Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. The 72 degC alarm comes before the 80 degC trip. A failing cabinet fan is often audible before the trip.
On ST30, check coolant flow first: a servo temperature rise that follows a fall in coolant flow is a cooling-circuit problem (see Section 6.4), not a drive problem.
A servo temperature rise with normal coolant flow and a cabinet fan that is noisy, slow or stopped points to the cabinet cooling fan or a clogged cabinet filter.

citations.quote: Regulated gun air (`air_pressure_bar`) normally sits at 5.6 bar within 5.3 to 5.9 bar. Below 5 bar the cell raises a low-air alarm; at 4.6 bar the supply-air interlock stops the cell. Gun force alarms (A-ST20-GUN-FRC, A-ST30-GUN-FRC) can appear as the air falls.

When gun air pressure falls at ST20 and ST30 together, the cause is upstream in the plant air supply; check the header pressure (see Section 6.2 of AM-CA-01 (Plant Air System and Utilities)) before working on either cell.
When gun air falls at one cell only, check that cell's filter-regulator, drop-leg ball valve and quick couplings.

citations.quote: A narrow bead with normal flow and pressure points to the nozzle or the bead program; a narrow bead with low flow points to the pump supply (see Section 6.2).
| Bead narrow, flow and pressure normal | Nozzle tip partly blocked with cured material | Inspect the nozzle tip | Clean or replace the nozzle tip |
| Pressure high, flow low, no pulsing | Hose or nozzle partly blocked | Purge the nozzle; check the pressure drop along the hose | Clean the nozzle; replace the hose if blocked |

Outlet pressure (`pump_pressure_bar`) starts to pulse at the pump stroke rate (0.15 Hz, one stroke about every 6.7 s) and its mean falls. Flow (`flow_rate_ccm`) drops below its normal range of 270 to 330 cc/min. Motor current falls slightly and becomes unsteady because the pump moves less material. The bead becomes narrow and uneven (A-ST40-BEAD-QA) and ST60 rejects rise.

citations.quote: | S-ST20-SRV-OT / S-ST30-SRV-OT | servo drive over-temperature trip | Drive stopped the cell; see Section 6.3 |

Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. The 72 degC alarm comes before the 80 degC trip. A failing cabinet fan is often audible before the trip.

| Trip S-ST20-SRV-OT or S-ST30-SRV-OT at 80 degC | Sustained overheating not corrected at the alarm stage | Check coolant flow (ST30), the cabinet fan and the gun mechanics for binding | Let the drive cool; restart only after the cause is found |

This derating penalty adds 0.8 s to cycle duration for every degree Celsius above 66 degC. As speed falls, cell cycle time rises past the nominal 50 s standard, causing downstream starvation. If temperature reaches 72 degC, the cell issues an over-temperature alarm, followed by a total cell trip at 80 degC. An audible cabinet fan problem often precedes the trip.

Hydraulic component degradation develops slowly over hours or days of continuous production, contrasting sharply with immediate changeover parameter steps. Four primary physical mechanisms drive this wear: variable pump internal leakage, switching valve lag, loss of bladder accumulator nitrogen precharge, and reduced oil cooler efficiency. As internal clearances in the pump widen, slip flow returns directly to the tank instead of the main line, reducing available volume under load.

Hydraulic wear develops over hours to days, not at a changeover. Four failure modes are common: internal pump leakage, a sluggish (lagging) switching valve, loss of accumulator precharge, and loss of cooler efficiency. citations.quote: Regulated gun air (`air_pressure_bar`) normally sits at 5.6 bar within 5.3 to 5.9 bar. Below 5 bar the cell raises a low-air alarm; at 4.6 bar the supply-air interlock stops the cell. Gun force alarms (A-ST20-GUN-FRC, A-ST30-GUN-FRC) can appear as the air falls.

citations.quote: When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows. The weld cells see their regulated gun air fall shortly after; gun force alarms follow, and when gun air reaches each cell's own low limit (see the weld cell manual) the supply-air interlock stops that cell.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

| Header pressure low, compressor current low (not loading) | Inlet valve stuck closed, or load control fault | Check the compressor display for load status and faults | Repair the inlet valve or load control |

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

| Header pressure low, compressor current low (not loading) | Inlet valve stuck closed, or load control fault | Check the compressor display for load status and faults | Repair the inlet valve or load control |

Four failure modes are common: internal pump leakage, a sluggish (lagging) switching valve, loss of accumulator precharge, and loss of cooler efficiency. | Failure mode | Main pressure | Motor current | Oil temperature | Vibration | Cycle time |

| Accumulator precharge loss | Slow swing (about 20 s period), noisy | Fluctuates | Normal | Normal | Longer |
| Cooler efficiency loss | Normal | Normal | Rises steadily | Normal | Slightly longer |

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

citations.quote: Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. The 72 degC alarm comes before the 80 degC trip. A failing cabinet fan is often audible before the trip.
On ST30, check coolant flow first: a servo temperature rise that follows a fall in coolant flow is a cooling-circuit problem (see Section 6.4), not a drive problem.
A servo temperature rise with normal coolant flow and a cabinet fan that is noisy, slow or stopped points to the cabinet cooling fan or a clogged cabinet filter.

| Trip S-ST20-SRV-OT or S-ST30-SRV-OT at 80 degC | Sustained overheating not corrected at the alarm stage | Check coolant flow (ST30), the cabinet fan and the gun mechanics for binding | Let the drive cool; restart only after the cause is found |

citations.quote: Typical signature. Coolant flow (coolant_flow_lpm, ST30 only) falls below its normal range of 10 to 14 L/min and the 8 L/min low alarm follows. With less cooling, servo temperature starts to rise about 15 minutes later, then the drive derates (cycle time rises) and finally trips on over-temperature. Weld current becomes noisier as the electrodes run hot.
Falling coolant flow followed some minutes later by rising servo temperature identifies a restricted coolant circuit; a servo temperature rise without any flow change does not.
Coolant flow that falls at ST30 while the chiller supply temperature stays normal points to a restriction inside the cell (strainer, kinked hose, scaled gun passages), not to the chiller.
| coolant_flow_lpm below 10 L/min | Cell strainer clogged | Read the strainer differential gauge; inspect the strainer basket | Clean the strainer basket under energy control (Chapter 8) |

citations.quote: | S-ST10-HYD-FLT | ST10 Press: hydraulic fault, press stopped | Hydraulic protection; see Section 6.3 |

Hydraulic wear develops over hours to days, not at a changeover. Four failure modes are common: internal pump leakage, a sluggish (lagging) switching valve, loss of accumulator precharge, and loss of cooler efficiency.

Each moves pressure, motor current, oil temperature, vibration and cycle time in its own pattern; use Table 6-3 to tell them apart. All four lengthen the press cycle, which starves the stations downstream.
